reason: The sources provide more than 10 highly surprising, cross-verified facts about 2019 OK's sudden discovery and its hair-raising near-miss.
story: In July 2019, a massive space rock named 2019 OK caught planetary defenders completely off guard. Roughly the size of a football field, this "city-killer" asteroid was officially announced just hours before its closest approach. It screamed past Earth at nearly 55,000 miles per hour, missing us by less than one-fifth of the distance to the Moon. If it had struck, it could have exploded with over 30 times the energy of the Hiroshima atomic bomb, devastating an area 50 miles wide. Why didn't we see it? Existing sky surveys had actually photographed it weeks prior, but missed it because its highly elliptical orbit had it heading directly towards us. This made it appear completely stationary in the night sky. Thankfully, this Apollo-class asteroid won't return this close for another 200 years, giving humanity time to build better celestial eyes.
angle: A football-field-sized asteroid sneaked past Earth closer than the Moon, going undetected until the last minute because it was heading directly at us, making it appear completely stationary in the sky.

claims.claim: The near-Earth asteroid is officially designated 2019 OK.
The asteroid is estimated to be roughly the size of a football field, or between 57 and 130 meters (187 to 426 feet) in diameter.
The asteroid safely flew past Earth on July 24 or 25, 2019.
Its closest approach brought it within less than one-fifth of the distance to the Moon.
The asteroid traveled at a speed of nearly 55,000 miles per hour (about 88,500 kilometers per hour).
It was first discovered by amateur astronomers at the private SONEAR Observatory in Brazil.
The SONEAR astronomers who detected it were Cristóvão Jacques, Eduardo Pimentel, and João Ribeiro.
Its discovery was officially confirmed and publicly announced only hours before its closest approach.
Telescopes like Pan-STARRS had actually photographed the asteroid weeks prior, but it was not recognized.
It went unrecognized in early survey images because its apparent motion was extremely slow as it headed directly towards Earth.
If the asteroid had impacted Earth, it could have released over 30 times the energy of the Hiroshima atomic bomb.
The asteroid has a highly elliptical orbit that takes it from within the orbit of Venus to well beyond Mars.
It completes one orbit around the Sun approximately every 2.7 years (roughly 932 to 993 days).
It is officially classified as an Apollo-class asteroid.
The asteroid will not make another close flyby to Earth of this proximity for at least another 200 years.
The initial SONEAR detection was independently confirmed by other telescopes, including the ISON network.

disputed: The exact closest approach distance is disputed. Sources S1, S6, and S7 list it around 71,354 kilometers (44,337 miles), S2 and S3 state about 65,000 kilometers (40,000 miles), while S4 and S5 state about 45,000 miles (72,500 kilometers). The script should describe the distance generally as 'between 40,000 and 45,000 miles.'

Some news sources (S4, S5) attribute the late detection to the asteroid approaching from the direction of the Sun. However, astronomical records (S1, S3, S7) state the actual reasons were its slow apparent motion, Southern Hemisphere positioning, and bright moonlight. The script should focus on its slow apparent motion making it look like a star.
